To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the humoral response of mice to gluten‐derived proteins is influenced by diet.
The influence of diet (gluten‐based versus maize‐based) on antibody responses was examined using ELISA and immunoblotting techniques.

(1) diet influences the specificity, aswell as the magnitude of serum antibody responses in mice immunized with cereal proteins, (2) oral tolerance to gluten and maize proteins is not absolute and (3) oral tolerance appears to affect the humoral response of some cereal proteins morethan others.

the development of a novel method of immunization forthe production of high titre antibodies.
the immunological basis of the coeliac disease and its relationship to the ingestion of wheat and other cereals.
understanding the mechanisms of oral tolerance to dietary antigens, with the aim of identifying those factors which are important in the development and maintenance of food‐sensitive disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the results of the present investigation indicate that the diet of the mouse can influence both the magnitude and the specificity of the humoral immune response to gluten and to maize protein fractions.

the immunological response of the gut to gluten is complex and is influenced by many factors including the diet, the genetic background of the individual, the presence of other food antigens and the nature of the gluten preparation used for oral or parenteral immunization.

(i) oral tolerance to gluten proteins is diet dependent; (ii) oral tolerance to maize proteins is not diet dependent, but the response to alpha‐zein is more pronounced in the maize‐fed animals than the wheat‐fed animals, while the response to maize glutelin is the same; (iii) oral tolerance to wheat‐derived proteins is diet dependent.
